AMD Stock Is Up 131% This Year. Here's Where It Stands After a $1 Trillion Run ©vkstudio via Canva
Key Takeaways

AMD stock is up 131.3% since early January, closing at $516.79 on October 23, yet it trades 20.4% below its October 6 record close of $649.42 after a chip-sector selloff.

Wall Street sees normalized EPS climbing from $4.17 in 2025 to $7.59 in 2026 and $15.76 in 2027.

AMD reports third-quarter results on November 3, guiding for $13 billion in revenue.

The Street expects $22.82 in normalized EPS for 2028, above the $20 threshold in AMD's long-term non-GAAP earnings target. Lisa Su said in August that AMD now expects to significantly exceed that target.

Advanced Micro Devices (AMD:NASDAQ) stock is up 131.3% since early January, closing at $516.79 on October 23, after two record data center quarters carried the chipmaker from a February rout to a $1 trillion market value.

The last three weeks took a real bite out of that. AMD stock now sits 20.4% below its October 6 record close of $649.42 (by my math), and the damage came from a sector selloff rather than anything AMD reported. What's left is a stock priced on a 2027 earnings jump that hasn't happened yet.

AMD Stock Started 2026 With a 17% Gut Punch
AMD Stock Price, Year to Date (TIKR)

The year opened badly. AMD beat fourth-quarter estimates on February 3, but guided first-quarter revenue to $9.8 billion, plus or minus $300 million, below the record $10.27 billion it had just booked, and said sales of its MI308 chips to China would shrink to around $100 million from roughly $390 million. AMD stock shed 17.3% on February 4. By March 3, it sat 27.76% below its late-2025 peak.

The order that mattered most landed in between. On February 24, AMD and Meta Platforms (META:NASDAQ) agreed to deploy up to 6 gigawatts of Instinct GPUs over several chip generations, with first shipments due in the second half of 2026 and a performance-based warrant giving Meta the right to up to 160 million AMD shares. The climb itself started in April, when Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing (TSM:NYSE) reported 41% first-quarter sales growth and AMD shares rose 7.80% that day. By May 5, the stock traded in the mid-$350s.

AMD's May 5 report put first-quarter revenue at $10.25 billion against the $9.89 billion analysts expected, according to Reuters, with data center sales up 57% to a record $5.8 billion. It guided second-quarter revenue to $11.2 billion, plus or minus $300 million. AMD stock jumped 18.61% the next day and reached the mid-$580s by late June.

With $10,000, you can establish a meaningful position in a trio of semiconductor stocks that have the potential to lead the market higher over the next few years. In fact, by the end of 2030, a $10,000 investment spread equally among Nvidia (NASDAQ: NVDA), Advanced Micro Devices (NASDAQ: AMD), and Broadcom (NASDAQ: AVGO) could be worth roughly $29,000.

Now, for an investment in these three stocks to work, the AI infrastructure boom will have to continue. If it doesn't, these semiconductor stocks will likely fall well short of that potential. However, with hyperscalers (owners of large data centers) seeing strong returns on their AI infrastructure investments and expected to continue spending aggressively, this looks like a good bet.

Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 14x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue »

Let's see how a $10,000 investment in these AI stocks could more than triple by 2030.

Image source: Getty Images.
Nvidia (15.7 shares)

By splitting $10,000 evenly among the three stocks, you'd get 15.7 shares of Nvidia at the current $212.21 price. Nvidia's graphics processing units (GPUs) are the primary chips powering AI workloads, and the company holds a dominant position in AI training, as most early code was written on its CUDA software platform and optimized for its chips.

With Space Exploration Technologies and most neoclouds exclusively using its GPUs, the company still has huge growth ahead. Meanwhile, Nvidia is more than just a GPU company today, having transformed itself into a full-fledged AI infrastructure player whose networking portfolio, central processing units (CPUs), and inference chips can deliver end-to-end servers that provide turnkey solutions for specific AI tasks.

The current analyst consensus is for Nvidia to produce adjusted EPS of $28.79 in fiscal year 2031 (ending in January 2031). However, I think that is low, and the company could generate adjusted EPS close to $41.50 in fiscal year 2021 and $48.55 in fiscal year 2032. Using just a market multiple of 19 times (the S&P 500's forward P/E multiple), the stock could be worth around $922 by the end of 2030, and those 15.7 shares valued at $14,475.

title: 1 Red Flag That Keeps Me From Buying AMD Stock
detail:
1 Red Flag That Keeps Me From Buying AMD Stock
Keithen Drury, The Motley Fool
Sat, October 24, 2026 at 5:54 PM PDT 4 min read
AMD
NVDA
Explore stocks on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

AMD (NASDAQ: AMD) struggled in the early stages of the AI arms race. Its technology was lacking and behind its competition.

While I won't claim that AMD has caught up on the technological front, its products are far more competitive and serve as viable alternatives to other AI computing units, such as those from Nvidia.

Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 14x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue »

However, I'm still not planning on buying AMD stock anytime soon. Why? It's just too expensive. The reality is that a ton of growth has already been priced into the stock, and it's just too expensive to consider investing in right now.

Image source: The Motley Fool.
AMD is expensive by practically any valuation measure

The most common way to value a stock is to use the price-to-earnings (P/E) ratio. This utilizes earnings over the past 12 months to value the stock, and for a big tech company like AMD involved in the AI arms race, you'd probably expect it to be valued between 25 and 35 times earnings. But that's far from the case.

AMD PE Ratio data by YCharts

At 130 times earnings, AMD is a very expensive stock. However, one may argue that its profit margins are improving rapidly compared with a few quarters ago. I'll buy this argument, but if I value it based on forward earnings, which should include more optimized quarters, it's still very expensive.

AMD PE Ratio (Forward) data by YCharts

Consider that 67 times forward earnings is a very pricey tag, and it's far higher than AMD has previously been valued.

As a final argument, AMD bulls may point to how strong a year AMD expects in 2027. I don't disagree that it will be a great year for AMD as a company, but the reality is that all of 2027's growth is already priced into AMD's stock.

AMD PE Ratio (Forward 1y) data by YCharts

At 32 times next year's earnings, AMD basically has a year and a half of growth priced into its stock right now. So, if AMD hits all analyst expectations and its stock stays flat until next year's results are finalized, AMD will trade at a reasonable 32 times trailing earnings.

That's just too much growth to pay up for right now, especially considering that its primary competitor, Nvidia, trades at 27 times trailing earnings. I think AMD's stock is overextending and way out in front of its skis, and either two things will happen over the next year.

First, it could experience a sizable sell-off. Second, it could underperform as it grows into its valuation. Neither of those two options is attractive, so I'm staying away from AMD stock.

title: Here's Why AMD Investors Should Consider Selling Before Nov. 3
detail:
Here's Why AMD Investors Should Consider Selling Before Nov. 3
Keithen Drury, The Motley Fool
Sat, October 24, 2026 at 4:33 AM PDT 4 min read
AMD
NVDA
^GSPC
Explore stocks on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

AMD (NASDAQ: AMD) has been a tremendous stock to own in 2026. It has risen about 150% this year, ranking in the top 10 for best-performing S&P 500 (SNPINDEX: ^GSPC) stocks. That's an admirable performance, and it has AMD investors believing that it's truly taking ground from primary competitor Nvidia (NASDAQ: NVDA) in the all-important data center market.

However, I think some of this performance isn't earned, and the stock could be ripe for a pullback. There are several factors that point to this potentially coming, and getting out of the stock before AMD's Nov. 3 earnings report could save investors from some heartache.

Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue »

Image source: The Motley Fool.
AMD's stock is very expensive

At face value, AMD's stock is not cheap, regardless of which valuation measure you use.

AMD PE Ratio (Forward) data by YCharts. PE = price-to-earnings.

At nearly 140 times trailing earnings, it's very pricey for the results it has delivered. Even at 70 times this year's earnings, it's still expensive. Analysts expect a huge year next year, with it trading at 34 times next year's earnings, but that's still just a very expensive stock, especially when compared to Nvidia.

Nvidia is AMD's nemesis in the data center space, and these two have competed against each other for a long time. Nvidia has nearly always been the winner, but from an investment standpoint, that has shifted in 2026. However, I don't think that has really been earned.

AMD's price tag has increased dramatically throughout the year, as evidenced by the chart above. While AMD trades for 34 times next year's earnings, Nvidia trades for 27 times trailing earnings. That's right, Nvidia is cheaper right now than AMD is projected to be at the end of next year if its stock price stays flat.

That's a huge pricing mismatch for companies in the same industry, and I think all of that could come to a head during AMD's third-quarter results.

AMD needs to continue accelerating its growth to justify its price

During AMD's second-quarter results, it reported accelerating data center revenue, rising 107% year over year to $6.7 billion. However, overall company revenue accelerated at just a 50% pace to $11.5 billion. That's because AMD's non-data center business units didn't have great quarters, and they are a drag on AMD's overall financial picture.

Credo Technology Group is showcasing its OmniConnect Weaver memory gearbox on AMD's Versal AI Edge Series Gen 2 platform and has detailed a 1.6T ZeroFlap active light cable and a new OCP workstream for Short-Reach Micro-Emitter Optics that target future AI data center interconnect needs.

In the same week that these products and collaborations were highlighted, fresh commentary about rising competition in active electrical cables and slower 1.6T adoption raised questions about how quickly Credo can convert its pipeline into durable revenue.

We will now look at how Credo Technology Group's investment narrative could be affected by rising AEC competition around 1.6T connectivity.

Scan beyond Credo Technology Group Holding and compare it with 55 AI infrastructure stocks that are also wiring the AI buildout inside data centers.

Credo Technology Group Holding Investment Narrative Recap

To own Credo Technology Group Holding, you need to believe AI data centers will keep requiring denser, more power efficient wiring and that Credo can stay relevant as speeds climb and media shifts from copper to optics. The immediate swing factor is how quickly its AEC demand turns into repeat orders while competition around 1.6T ramps. The fresh MaxLinear comments and share pullback mostly hit sentiment rather than Credo's underlying design wins.

The biggest operational risk is that heavy AI buildouts slow or key hyperscalers pause deployments, which could expose revenue concentration and high R&D spend. Rising rivals in both AECs and optics raise the chance of pricing pressure if 1.6T adoption proves slower than expected. Credo's near term setup depends on converting its product pipeline into shipping volume before competitors narrow its technical or power efficiency gap.

The new 1.6T ZeroFlap active light cable looks most relevant to the current debate. It directly addresses questions about how Credo participates if the market tilts toward optics instead of AECs at higher speeds. Shipping is guided for 2027, so this is not solving today's revenue lumpiness, but it clarifies how the business is preparing for rack to rack AI fabrics beyond the current AEC cycle.

For an investor, that cable and the Short Reach Micro Emitter Optics workstream together frame a practical catalyst. If Credo can prove reliable, low power 1.6T optical links in real AI data center trials, it gives the product story more breadth against both MaxLinear in AEC silicon and larger optical incumbents. Execution risk is real, since any delay in the OCP specification or in qualifying ZeroFlap could leave Credo more exposed to slower 1.6T spending while expenses stay elevated.

What Happened?

Advanced Micro Devices (AMD:NASDAQ) closed at $507.93 on October 22, down 8.10%, a day after Susquehanna raised its price target to $620 from $550. Most coverage tied the drop to Lam Research (LRCX), a chipmaking equipment supplier that said supply constraints held down its guidance. AMD fell harder than the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index, down 6.72%, and NVIDIA (NVDA), down 4.40%. It had already slid about 15% from its October 6 record close of $649.42 before the warning and closed October 22 at 21.79% below that record.

AMD Drawdowns (TIKR)
Three Signals Cut the Multiple

Lam CFO Doug Bettinger said the $8.6 billion revenue guide "would have been a bit higher if not for some near-term supply chain constraints," and reports on the October 21 call put Lam's supply-chain and clean-room limits into 2027. At NVIDIA's GTC Berlin event, CEO Jensen Huang called neocloud demand off the charts but said those buyers lack the working capital to fund it. Meta Platforms (META), one of AMD's 6-gigawatt GPU customers, fell 6.98% the day after its third-quarter report.

None of that has reached AMD's forecasts yet. Between September 30 and October 22, AMD's NTM P/E fell from about 55x to about 46x, per TIKR, while its NTM normalized EPS estimate held near $11 and the 2027 revenue consensus rose about 1%. The roughly 17% price drop came entirely from the multiple. AMD still trades at more than twice the ~18x of NVIDIA and the ~19x of Broadcom (AVGO), with consensus normalized EPS growing around 94% a year from 2025 to 2027.

AMD NTM Price / Normalized Earnings (TIKR)

TIKR tracks 55 analysts on AMD. How many say "Buy"? See the full breakdown of Buy, Hold, and Sell ratings on AMD, along with Wall Street's revenue and earnings estimates, all in one place. More than 500,000 investors use TIKR to research stocks like this one. See AMD's Analyst Ratings

Rack Timing Is Where the Forecasts Are Exposed

At the Goldman Sachs Communacopia + Technology Conference on September 11, Dan McNamara, AMD's SVP and general manager of Compute Enterprise AI, said "getting rack scale solutions at scale is the biggest thing we're focused on right now." Later in the session, looking 12 to 24 months out, he said, "I think it will become very clear how we have made that transition quickly."

That window overlaps the period Lam flagged. Meta's first gigawatt, with shipments scheduled to begin in the second half of 2026, is built on AMD's Helios rack-scale architecture. As of September 11, McNamara still saw demand running ahead of plan, saying of AMD's November analyst-day CPU forecast, "we called it too low."

Investors interested in Computer - Integrated Systems stocks are likely familiar with Micron (MU) and Advanced Micro Devices (AMD). But which of these two stocks presents investors with the better value opportunity right now? Let's take a closer look.

We have found that the best way to discover great value opportunities is to pair a strong Zacks Rank with a great grade in the Value category of our Style Scores system. The proven Zacks Rank puts an emphasis on earnings estimates and estimate revisions, while our Style Scores work to identify stocks with specific traits.

Right now, Micron is sporting a Zacks Rank of #1 (Strong Buy), while Advanced Micro Devices has a Zacks Rank of #3 (Hold). This means that MU's earnings estimate revision activity has been more impressive, so investors should feel comfortable with its improving analyst outlook. But this is just one factor that value investors are interested in.

Value investors are also interested in a number of tried-and-true valuation metrics that help show when a company is undervalued at its current share price levels.

The Value category of the Style Scores system identifies undervalued companies by looking at a number of key metrics. These include the long-favored P/E ratio, P/S ratio, earnings yield, cash flow per share, and a variety of other fundamentals that help us determine a company's fair value.

MU currently has a forward P/E ratio of 4.82, while AMD has a forward P/E of 67.28. We also note that MU has a PEG ratio of 0.15. This figure is similar to the commonly-used P/E ratio, with the PEG ratio also factoring in a company's expected earnings growth rate. AMD currently has a PEG ratio of 4.49.

Another notable valuation metric for MU is its P/B ratio of 6.99. The P/B ratio pits a stock's market value against its book value, which is defined as total assets minus total liabilities. For comparison, AMD has a P/B of 12.34.

These metrics, and several others, help MU earn a Value grade of B, while AMD has been given a Value grade of F.

MU has seen stronger estimate revision activity and sports more attractive valuation metrics than AMD, so it seems like value investors will conclude that MU is the superior option right now.
